headline: Dow closes above 2,000 for the first time
text: The Dow Jones Industrial Average, the best-known index of big American shares, closed above 2,000 for the first time on 8 January. A rising market has carried it to new highs.

headline: Tokyo's Nikkei index passes 20,000
text: Japan's Nikkei 225 share index closed above 20,000 for the first time on 30 January. The Bank of Japan has cut its main interest rate from 5 percent towards 2.5 percent, and cheap money is pushing up shares and land prices. Big lenders such as the Industrial Bank of Japan are at the centre of the boom.

headline: Disneyland opens Star Tours, a Star Wars flight simulator
text: Disney opened Star Tours at Disneyland on 9 January, a ride made with George Lucas in which visitors take a bumpy simulated flight through the Star Wars universe. Disney bought four military-grade flight simulators at $500,000 each, and the ride cost $32 million in all. The opening was celebrated with a 60-hour marathon.

headline: Six rich countries agree in Paris to steady the dollar
text: Finance ministers of six leading economies signed the Louvre Accord in Paris on 22 February. The dollar has lost more than a quarter of its value against other main currencies and stands near 150 yen. The countries promise to work together to stop it falling further, with Japan cutting interest rates and others trimming budget deficits.

headline: Two Kidder Peabody traders arrested for insider trading
text: Richard Wigton and Timothy Tabor of Kidder, Peabody were arrested at their office on 11 February and charged, along with a Goldman Sachs partner, with trading on secret takeover information. General Electric bought Kidder last year. The government's case relies on Martin Siegel, a former Kidder dealmaker who has turned witness.

headline: Japan starts selling shares in its phone monopoly NTT
text: Shares in Nippon Telegraph and Telephone, Japan's state-owned phone company, began trading in Tokyo on 10 February at 1.6 million yen each. The government sold the first lot by auction at an average winning bid of 1.197 million yen. It is a big step in privatising a state-owned company.

headline: A star explodes, visible to the naked eye
text: Astronomers spotted the supernova SN 1987A on 23 February. It is the first exploding star that can be seen without a telescope since 1604.

headline: Apple launches the Macintosh II, the first Mac in colour
text: Apple introduced the Macintosh II in March, the first Mac with colour graphics and internal expansion slots. It is a box with a separate monitor on top, more like an IBM-style PC than the earlier all-in-one Macs. A basic system with monitor and 20 MB disk costs about $5,498, which puts it in reach of businesses and designers, not families.

headline: Channel ferry capsizes off Zeebrugge, 193 dead
text: The cross-Channel ferry Herald of Free Enterprise capsized near the Belgian port of Zeebrugge on 6 March. The death toll was 193.

headline: Chrysler buys American Motors
text: Chrysler acquired American Motors Corporation on 2 March. American Motors is the maker of Jeep.

headline: Physicists hold a 'Woodstock' for superconductors
text: On 18 March physicists gathered for a packed meeting on superconductors that was nicknamed the Woodstock of physics. Superconductors are materials that carry electric current with no resistance.

headline: IBM launches the PS/2 range of personal computers
text: IBM unveiled its Personal System/2 on 2 April, a new family that succeeds the PC, XT and AT. The machines use 3.5-inch floppy disks and a new graphics standard called VGA, and the higher-end models use IBM's own Micro Channel design, which others may copy only on licence terms.

headline: Microsoft and IBM announce the OS/2 operating system
text: On 2 April Microsoft and IBM announced OS/2, a new operating system for the new IBM machines and the first product from the joint development deal the two signed in August 1985. At launch, only the older PC DOS 3.3 is actually available to buy.

headline: Andy Grove named chief executive of Intel
text: Intel named Andy Grove chief executive on 28 April, with co-founder Gordon Moore staying on as chairman. The company introduced the 386, its first 32-bit processor, in 1985, in the middle of the worst downturn the chip business had known.

headline: Fox starts a TV network, and The Simpsons arrive as shorts
text: The new Fox network began prime-time programming on 5 April. On 19 April a series of short cartoons about a yellow family, the Simpsons, debuted as part of The Tracey Ullman Show.

headline: Iraqi missiles hit USS Stark, 37 sailors die
text: Iraqi missiles struck the American frigate USS Stark in the Persian Gulf on 17 May, killing 37 sailors. The Gulf is a war zone between Iran and Iraq.

headline: Gary Hart quits the race for US president
text: Gary Hart was a leading candidate for the Democratic nomination. He dropped out of the 1988 presidential race on 8 May.

headline: 800,000 walk the Golden Gate Bridge at its 50th birthday
text: About 800,000 people crowded San Francisco's Golden Gate Bridge on 24 May to celebrate its 50th anniversary. The same day Al Unser won his fourth Indianapolis 500.

headline: Nikkei passes 25,000
text: Tokyo's Nikkei 225 closed above 25,000 for the first time on 3 June, only a few months after crossing 20,000 in January. Low interest rates continue to feed the rally in Japanese shares.

headline: Reagan at the Berlin Wall: 'tear down this wall'
text: Speaking in West Berlin on 12 June, President Reagan challenged Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev to 'tear down this wall'. Gorbachev has been talking about reform in the Soviet Union, and the West is watching to see if he means it.

headline: New York subway gunman Goetz cleared on most counts
text: A New York jury found Bernhard Goetz not guilty on 12 of 13 counts on 16 June, in the trial over his shooting of four youths on a subway train in December 1984. The case has split public opinion in New York.

headline: Dow closes above 2,500 for the first time
text: The Dow Jones Industrial Average closed at 2,510.04 on 17 July, the first time above 2,500. It first passed 2,000 only in January, so the climb has been fast.

headline: GE swaps its TV and radio business for a French medical firm
text: General Electric agreed to hand its consumer electronics business, mostly gained in last year's purchase of RCA, to France's Thomson. In return it gets Thomson's medical equipment division and some cash. The business sold about $3 billion of TVs, radios and video recorders last year, and the swap gives GE a foothold in the European medical-equipment market.

headline: Wal-Mart marks 25 years: 1,198 stores and $15.9 billion in sales
text: Wal-Mart celebrated its 25th birthday with 1,198 stores, $15.9 billion in sales and 200,000 employees, whom it calls associates. Its stores are linked by a satellite network, a $24 million investment carrying two-way voice and data, so headquarters can follow stock and sales.

headline: Edzard Reuter takes over at Daimler-Benz
text: Edzard Reuter became chairman of Daimler-Benz in July, succeeding Werner Breitschwerdt. Daimler already holds a majority of the electrical group AEG and stakes in Dornier and MTU. Reuter wants an integrated technology group that depends less on the ups and downs of the car and truck business.

headline: Microsoft buys Forethought, maker of PowerPoint
text: Microsoft bought Forethought on 30 July, the developer of PowerPoint, a leading program for making presentation slides. The purchase brings Microsoft a product for the Apple Macintosh as well as for IBM-style PCs.

headline: Alan Greenspan sworn in as head of the Federal Reserve
text: Alan Greenspan was sworn in on 11 August as chairman of the Federal Reserve, the American central bank that sets the cost of borrowing. He takes over as the dollar is weak and share prices are high.

headline: Dow sets another record close, 2,722.42
text: The Dow Jones Industrial Average closed at a record 2,722.42 on 25 August, just over five weeks after first passing 2,500. It closed above 2,000 for the first time only on 8 January.

headline: Apple's HyperCard lets ordinary users program their own Macs
text: Apple announced HyperCard on 11 August, a multimedia, easily programmed system for the Macintosh designed by Bill Atkinson. Atkinson agreed to hand it over to Apple only if it would be given away free with every Mac.

headline: Schlumberger sells its Fairchild chip business to National Semiconductor
text: Schlumberger, the oilfield-services group, sold its Fairchild Semiconductor chip business to National Semiconductor, announced on 31 August. Contemporary reports put the price at about $122 million in stock and warrants, against the $425 million Schlumberger paid in 1979.

headline: The Fed raises its lending rate to 6 percent
text: On 4 September the Federal Reserve raised the discount rate, the rate at which it lends to banks, from 5.5 to 6 percent. Higher rates make borrowing dearer across the economy and can cool share prices.

headline: Buffett puts $700 million into Salomon Brothers
text: On 27 September Warren Buffett's Berkshire Hathaway agreed to buy $700 million of Salomon Brothers preferred stock paying 9 percent and convertible into shares at $38. Salomon used a separate deal to buy back a 12 percent stake from Minorco for $809 million, which keeps it away from raider Ronald Perelman. Berkshire gets two seats on the board.

headline: BMW shows the Z1, a roadster with doors that drop into the sills
text: BMW unveiled the Z1 at the Frankfurt Motor Show in September, a two-seat sports car whose doors slide down into the body instead of swinging open. It has removable plastic body panels and uses the 2.5-litre six-cylinder engine of the 325i, giving 168 horsepower.

headline: Microsoft ships its first CD-ROM product
text: On 8 September Microsoft shipped Bookshelf, a collection of ten popular reference works on a single CD-ROM disc. A week later, on 14 September, it unveiled Works, an all-in-one program for home and small-business users.

headline: Black Monday: Dow falls 508 points, 22.6 percent in one day
text: On 19 October the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 508 points, or 22.6 percent, from 2,246.74 to 1,738.74, the biggest one-day percentage drop in its history. The S&P 500 index fell more than 20 percent. Blamed are worries about the dollar and trade deficit, rising interest rates and computer-driven selling.

headline: Stock markets crash around the world
text: The sell-off spread to every major market. Tokyo's Nikkei fell 14.9 percent on 20 October to 21,910, and Hong Kong closed its stock exchange for four working days. Over the month the markets of Hong Kong, Australia and Singapore fell by more than 40 percent.

headline: Fed promises cash and the market bounces, briefly
text: On the morning of 20 October Fed chairman Alan Greenspan said the Fed stood ready to supply cash to the financial system, and it put about $17 billion into bank reserves. Shares rallied by around 200 points, but the rebound did not last.

headline: Dow drops another 156 points as nerves stay raw
text: The Dow fell a further 156.83 points on 26 October. That came a week after Black Monday's 508-point fall, and showed that the crash had not cleared the air.

headline: Microsoft announces Excel for Windows
text: On 6 October Microsoft announced Excel for Windows, a spreadsheet program that runs inside its Windows desktop software. It is due to ship in November.

headline: Credit Suisse's US partner First Boston is hit by the crash
text: The October crash hit Credit Suisse First Boston, the Wall Street investment bank tied to Switzerland's Schweizerische Kreditanstalt, particularly hard. It has been dogged by internal disputes and a change at the top since 1986.

headline: Senate rejects Reagan's Supreme Court pick Robert Bork
text: The Senate voted 58 to 42 against Robert Bork on 23 October. President Reagan had nominated him to the Supreme Court on 1 July.

headline: Great storm batters southern England
text: On the night of 15 to 16 October one of the strongest storms in southern England in 200 years struck the region. People woke to wrecked trees and blocked roads, just days before the stock market crash dominated the news.

headline: Sony agrees to buy CBS Records for $2 billion
text: On 17 November Sony agreed to buy CBS Records, one of the world's biggest record companies, for $2 billion. The Japanese electronics group would get a big catalogue of recorded music.

headline: Iran-Contra reports blame Reagan for 'ultimate responsibility'
text: Reports on the Iran-Contra affair were published on 18 November. They put 'ultimate responsibility' for the scandal, a secret arms-for-hostages and rebel-funding scheme, on President Reagan.

headline: Fire at King's Cross station in London kills 31
text: A fire broke out at London's King's Cross underground station on 18 November. It killed 31 people.

headline: Excel for Windows goes on sale
text: Microsoft began shipping Excel for Windows on 19 November, a month after announcing it. Excel is meant to compete with Lotus 1-2-3, the market leader in spreadsheets.

headline: TV pirates hijack Chicago broadcasts
text: On 22 November someone interrupted two Chicago TV stations with a masked figure dressed as Max Headroom. Nobody was caught that night.

headline: A year after the Schweizerhalle fire, the Rhine is recovering
text: A year has passed since a fire at a Sandoz warehouse in Schweizerhalle near Basel sent firefighting water full of agrochemicals into the Rhine on 1 November 1986. A chemical-industry magazine reports that the river is recovering. Sandoz says it has extended its health, safety and environment programmes and introduced new emergency procedures.

headline: Reagan and Gorbachev sign the INF treaty
text: President Reagan and Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev signed the Intermediate-Range Nuclear Forces Treaty in Washington on 8 December. The treaty reduces nuclear stockpiles.

headline: Windows 2.0 ships to dealers
text: Microsoft shipped Windows 2.0 on 9 December. It lets programs sit in overlapping, resizable windows, costs $99 and comes with Windows versions of Word and Excel. A faster edition, Windows/386, can run several older DOS programs at once.

headline: Dow ends 1987 at 1,938.83, up 2 percent on the year
text: After October's crash the Dow Jones Industrial Average closed the year at 1,938.83, a gain of 2.26 percent over 1987. In August it had stood at a record 2,722.42.

headline: Palestinian unrest begins in Gaza and the West Bank
text: A wave of Palestinian protest against Israeli rule broke out in the Gaza Strip and West Bank in December. It is being called the intifada.

headline: Prozac goes on sale in the United States
text: The antidepressant Prozac debuted on the American market on 29 December. It was approved this year, as was the anti-AIDS drug AZT.
